clue.text: eg front part ten quite enough

parts.note: fore is the front part, as in the forepart of a ship
X is the Roman numeral for ten
ample means plentiful, quite enough

explanation.surface: A note jotted on the front of a page saying ten is plenty.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation eg stands for the Latin exempli gratia, introducing an illustration.

clue.text: Far from simple art one may produce

indicators.note: may produce suggests the letters can be worked into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Elaborate artwork that an artist might create.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaborately decorated, the opposite of plain.

clue.text: Somebody was willing to appoint him

definitions.text: Somebody was willing to appoint him

parts.words: Somebody was willing to appoint him
parts.note: willing here means making a will: the testator names the person who will carry it out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' looks like eager but means drawing up a will.
explanation.definitionFit: The person named in a will to administer the estate after death.

clue.text: No man's land.

parts.note: read as a land belonging to no man: Orwell's novel where animals oust the human owner

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means ground between trenches; here it is Orwell's 1945 fable in which the animals drive out the farmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's allegorical novel is set on a farm run by its livestock after the humans are expelled.

clue.text: under such control after novel rising

definitions.text: under such control after novel rising

parts.words: under such control after novel rising
parts.note: continues the previous clue: after the rebellion in that novel, the pigs take charge of the farm

explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this to 4 down: in Orwell's novel, after the animals' rising, the pigs end up in control.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to pigs, the rulers of Orwell's farm after the revolt.

clue.text: Slight advantage for side

explanation.definitionFit: A narrow lead over a rival, and also the border or rim of something.

clue.text: Capital chap adds six' more points to previous six

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals, placed first
six compass points: E, N, N, E, S, E

explanation.surface: A man in a city adds six to his score on top of an earlier six.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'points' are compass points, a convention for N, S, E and W; six of them follow the Roman VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Vienna, the Austrian capital.

clue.text: Prophet Hosea story is unusual

indicators.note: is unusual says the letters of the phrase are put into an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The tale of the Old Testament prophet Hosea is out of the ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: Hosea really is a prophet, which tempts as the definition; the definition is 'Prophet' and Hosea is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer who foretells the future.

clue.text: Cloak for masquerade spotted in play

explanation.surface: A disguise worn by a spotted character in a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' suggests the theatre, but the second sense is a game: the spotted tile used in a game of dominoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose hooded cloak with a half-mask worn at masked balls shares its name with a spotted tile used in a tabletop game.

clue.text: Put into rear, perhaps? More to the front, actually

indicators.note: put in the sense of set out or arranged, telling us the letters are rearranged
perhaps marks the arrangement as only one possible shuffling of the letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzling instruction to place something at the back, which turns out to mean the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' and 'perhaps' together signal that the letters of INTO REAR are rearranged; the paradox of rear versus front is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomists and grammarians use the word for something positioned further forward, nearer the front.

clue.text: Not original tail, we hear, for this horse

explanation.surface: A remark about a horse's unoriginal tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail, we hear' sounds like tale: a stale old joke or story. The horse is one of a reddish-brown colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A hackneyed story is called by the same word as a reddish-brown horse, named after the nut's colour.

clue.text: Number returned without Roman equivalent immediately after

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece surrounds the other
returned means the number's letters are read backwards

parts.note: ten is a number
X is the Roman numeral equivalent of ten

explanation.surface: A figure sent back because it lacks a Roman counterpart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside: TEN 'returned' gives NET, which goes round X, the Roman equivalent of that same number.
explanation.definitionFit: Following straight on, as in the person in the queue directly behind you.

clue.text: A minor, for example, has normal explanation

parts.note: natural means normal
a key explains, as to a map

explanation.surface: A youngster has a perfectly ordinary account of events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A minor' looks like a child, but it is the musical key with no sharps or flats.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical scale with no sharps or flats in its signature; A minor and C major are the two.

clue.text: Extended by generous bakers?

parts.note: bakers traditionally gave thirteen for twelve, so their batches of twelve were lengthened by one

explanation.walkthrough: A baker's dozen is thirteen; the old phrase for such stretched twelves is the answer, with long standing for extended.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old name for thirteen, the generous count bakers gave when selling by the dozen.

clue.text: European party without any standing

parts.note: Dutch means from the Netherlands, a European country
a treat is an outing or entertainment

explanation.surface: A political party from Europe that has no status at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' looks like status, but means paying for others, as in standing a round of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: An outing where each person pays their own share, so nobody stands anyone else a drink.

clue.text: Vent her malice — such a lot of hot air in Venice

indicators.note: taking a lot of, rather than all of, the words points to a run hidden inside them

explanation.surface: A Venetian woman venting her spite in a great blast of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such a lot of' points to letters inside 'Vent her malice'; 'in Venice' only dresses the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A thermal is a rising column of warmed air that gliders and birds ride upward.

clue.text: One using rod with acute distress?

definitions.text: One using rod with acute distress?

indicators.note: distress means the letters are knocked about into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who wields a cane, causing sharp pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, recalling schoolmasters with the cane, and also the wordplay, with 'distress' rearranging ROD and ACUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher of the old school wielded the cane as a disciplinary tool.

clue.text: Imposing arch frames Sir Henry

indicators.note: frames means one word is placed around another like a picture frame

parts.note: arch in the sense of knowing or cunning means sly
Sir Henry Tate, the sugar magnate who founded the Tate Gallery in London

explanation.surface: An impressive archway enclosing a statue of a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' looks architectural but means sly; Sir Henry Tate was the sugar refiner whose collection founded London's Tate Gallery, so his surname goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dignified and grand in manner is impressive, commanding respect.

clue.text: Won't change entrance room for public building

indicators.note: change says the letters of the word must be altered in order

parts.note: taken as written
a hall is the room you enter first

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to redecorate the lobby of a public building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges WON'T (the apostrophe drops) and the entrance room is HALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The building housing a local council's offices, used for civic meetings.

clue.text: Am immersed in endless source of Japanese paperwork

indicators.note: immersed in places the first piece inside the second
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: an origin is a source
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone deep in the bottomless origins of Japanese paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' drops the last letter of ORIGIN, leaving ORIGI, and 'immersed in' puts AM inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of folding paper into decorative shapes.

clue.text: Military exercise to change outer boundary

indicators.note: to change tells us the letters of the next word are altered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a march is a border region, as in the Welsh Marches

explanation.surface: Troops drilled to redraw the perimeter of their base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To change' rearranges OUTER; a march is an old word for a border district, as in the Welsh Marches.
explanation.definitionFit: A training walk in which soldiers cover a long distance in loose formation.

clue.text: River garb

explanation.definitionFit: The Wear is a river in north-east England flowing through Durham, and clothing in general is also called by this word.

clue.text: A hard wash here

parts.note: stern means hard or severe

explanation.surface: A tough laundry session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wash' looks like laundry but is the churned water a ship leaves behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel's wake trails behind it, at the back of the boat.

clue.text: Bound to join J Fisher in game

parts.note: to bound is to leap
Jeremy Fisher is the frog in Beatrix Potter's children's tale

explanation.surface: Someone obliged to go fishing with a man named J Fisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'obliged' but means a jump; Mr Jeremy Fisher is the frog in Beatrix Potter's story.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's playground pastime in which players vault over one another's bent backs.

clue.text: 22 in this Parliament?

definitions.meaning: the solution to 22 down, meaning at the back, points to the hindquarters
the 1648 to 1653 remnant of the Long Parliament after Pride's Purge

explanation.definitionFit: The hindquarters or rear end, and the name of the purged Parliament left sitting after 1648.

clue.text: Means to declare before very long

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the second in the answer

parts.note: to aver is to declare or assert
ages means a very long time

explanation.surface: Someone wanting to make a statement well in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means' looks like a verb but is the plural noun for mathematical middles.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics a mean is the arithmetic central value of a set, so the plural noun names several such values.

clue.text: Putting number one first? 1 is in order

parts.note: the clue for 1 across is the abbreviation eg, so the number stands for those letters

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether the top-ranked item is placed correctly at the head of a list.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' refers to 1 across, whose clue is just 'eg'; OM is Britain's Order of Merit, an honour, and IS goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-centredness means always looking after oneself before anyone else.

clue.text: Direct with nothing on, on stage

indicators.note: on in an across clue places the second piece after the first

parts.note: a point is a stage reached, as in at this point
a blank is nothing, an empty space

explanation.surface: An actor performing naked on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a nude performance; 'nothing' is BLANK, set after POINT, a stage in a process.
explanation.definitionFit: Blunt and straightforward, like a shot fired from very close range.
